summary: This Wikipedia-style note gives an overview of education across several dimensions: preschool and kindergarten for ages roughly three to seven, the OECD's three forms of learning with emphasis on informal learning, and the historical rise of US secondary education. It also covers barriers to Universal Primary Education, including funding, corruption and parental economic pressure, and closes with the relationship between intelligence and educational attainment.
one_line: Overview of education covering preschool and kindergarten, informal learning, US secondary education history, Universal Primary Education barriers, and intelligence.
key_facts: Preschools provide education from ages approximately three to seven, depending on the country, before children enter primary education.
Preschools are also known as nursery schools and as kindergarten, except in the US, where kindergarten is a term used for primary education.
Kindergarten is described as providing a child-centered, preschool curriculum for three- to seven-year-old children.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) defines informal learning as one of three forms of learning.
Informal learning occurs at home, at work, and through daily interactions and shared relationships among members of society.
Secondary education in the United States did not emerge until 1910, with the rise of large corporations and advancing technology in factories.
In the US, high schools were created with a curriculum focused on practical job skills to prepare students for white collar or skilled blue collar work.
Universal Primary Education is one of the eight international Millennium Development Goals.

Researchers at the Overseas Development Institute indicated that main obstacles to education funding include conflicting donor priorities, an immature aid architecture, and a lack of evidence and advocacy.
Transparency International has identified corruption in the education sector as a major stumbling block to achieving Universal Primary Education in Africa.
Indigenous governments are reluctant to take on the ongoing costs involved in expanding education.
Some parents prefer their children to earn money in the short term rather than work towards the long-term benefits of education.
Individuals with higher intelligence tend to perform better at school and go on to higher levels of education.
Education increases measurable intelligence, according to the note.
Intelligence at age 53 is more closely correlated to intelligence at age 8 than to educational attainment.
